# FedVerify live demo: presenter script (5 minutes)

*Generated by `python3 -m fedverify.analysis.make_demo_md` from the results files; edit the template in that file,
not this one. Numbers below come from the last demo run (results/demo/heart_ours_lr_demo/seed0) and from the study's results.*

## Before the session (10 minutes earlier)

1. Terminal 1, the dashboard API: `cd backend && python3 app.py` (leave it running; it serves http://localhost:5000).
2. Terminal 2, the dashboard page: `cd frontend && python3 -m http.server 8080`, then open http://localhost:8080 in
   the browser. The Federated tab needs no account; if the sign-in window opens, sign in or close it.
3. Terminal 3, at the repository root: the command for step 2 below, typed but not run.
4. Have the fallback ready (end of this page) and the showcase page open in a second browser tab:
   `fedverify/results/showcase/index.html` (works offline).

## The 5 minutes

| Time | Do | Say (one sentence) | What it proves |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0:00 | Nothing yet. | "Four hospitals train one heart-disease model together; patient records never leave a hospital, and every update is signed and written to a blockchain." | The problem and the claim. |
| 0:20 | Run `python3 -m fedverify.survival.demo --push` in terminal 3. | "This is a real federated run, not a recording: it takes about 3 seconds." | It runs end to end on a laptop, with no network. |
| 0:40 | Point at the Set-up block. | "The threshold that decides what counts as poisoned, tau = 3.21, is read from the calibration file, never typed in." | Screening is calibrated, not hand-tuned. |
| 1:00 | Point at Round 1. | "Each hospital signs its update; the server checks every signature, builds one Merkle root for the round and mines it into a block." | Who contributed what, in this round, is fixed on the ledger. |
| 1:30 | Point at Round 2. | "Switzerland flips the sign of its update; the screen rejects it because an unusual share of its weights are outliers (s_coord = 3.37, above tau)." | A poisoned update is caught before it reaches the model, and the reason is recorded. |
| 2:00 | Point at Round 3. | "Someone replays an old signed update and someone signs with another hospital's key: the ledger rejects both, before any screening." | Double spending and endpoint compromise are stopped by checks, not by statistics. |
| 2:30 | Point at the Audit block. | "Anyone can take a stored update and check it against the root in the block; flip a single bit and the check fails." | The record cannot be edited after the fact without detection. |
| 3:00 | Browser, Federated tab: Refresh, then pick "UCI heart demo K=4 · Sign flip 25% · forensics · ε=4 · 3r". | "The dashboard shows the same run: who attacked, when, and what the screen did." | The banner names the attacker and the round; the grid shows round 2 caught and no honest hospital excluded. |
| 3:30 | Click **Verify proof** on round 3. | "The browser recomputes the proof itself; with the local chain it can only say the server's root is consistent, with Algorand it checks the public ledger too." | Inclusion is checkable without trusting the server (fully so with `--chain-backend algorand`). |
| 4:00 | Showcase tab: Results, then Poisoning. | "Across the full study the screen catches only a minority of attacker rounds, and we say so." | The demo catch is real but not typical: see question 1. |
| 4:40 | Stop. | "What the chain proves is who sent what and that nothing was changed afterwards, not that the average was computed correctly." | The honest limit: see question 3. |

## Three likely questions, with short honest answers

**1. Why is screening recall so low with 4–5 hospitals?** Screen recall is low: with K = 4 hospitals, recall on UCI heart disease is 13–27% over every attack and model; with K = 5 hospitals, recall on TCGA-BRCA is 9–99% over every attack and model. Most attacker hospital-rounds are not excluded, so the screen limits rather than prevents poisoning. A robust z-score needs a crowd to stand out
from: with four hospitals of very different sizes and outcome rates, an honest but unusual hospital looks as odd as
an attacker, so the threshold that keeps false alarms at 5.0% of honest rounds in calibration lets most attacks
through. Screening a
clean run still excludes 10.6–19.9% of honest hospital-rounds on UCI heart disease and 5.4–12.2% on TCGA-BRCA. In the demo,
round 2 is caught; with another seed it may not be, and the demo says so when it happens.

**2. Why does differential privacy hurt TCGA so much?** On TCGA-BRCA the pooled C-index falls from 0.574 without DP
to 0.507–0.520 with DP-SGD (ε = 1, 2, 4, 8), while UCI heart disease keeps a ROC-AUC of 0.843–0.857 at ε = 1, 2, 4, 8 against
0.859 without DP. TCGA has only 76 deaths among 474 patients (A8 has
4 deaths), so the model leans on up-weighting the rare deaths, and DP-SGD clips every example's gradient to a
fixed norm (C = 1): a death's up-weighted gradient is clipped back to the same size as a survivor's, which cancels
most of that weighting. That is why even the weakest privacy setting stays far below no DP: a near-noiseless smoke
run lost most of the gain too, so the cost looks like clipping more than noise (a clip-only ablation is still open,
TODO.md). The guarantee is per training example, and the realised epsilon stays at or under the target
(0.94 for 1, 1.89 for 2, 3.78 for 4, 7.56 for 8). Be careful with the size of the drop: paired with no DP on the same folds, the 95% bootstrap
intervals of the C-index difference are ε = 1: -0.135 to +0.004; ε = 2: -0.126 to +0.000; ε = 4: -0.111 to -0.003; ε = 8: -0.106 to -0.003, so with only 76 deaths only ε = 4, ε = 8 are distinguishably worse than no DP at this sample size; the others are not distinguishable from it.

**3. What does the blockchain NOT prove?** It proves which signed updates went into each round and that none was
changed afterwards. It does not prove that the server averaged them correctly (no verifiable aggregation), that a
hospital's data or training was honest (a signed update can still be poisoned: that is the screen's job), or that
a stolen key was not used by its thief. The local chain is one node on one laptop; only the Algorand option puts the
root on a public ledger. THREAT_MODEL.md lists every case.

## If something fails live (fallback)

- The demo errors: show the saved output of the last good run,
  `cat fedverify/results/demo/heart_ours_lr_demo/fallback/demo_output.txt`, and talk through it with the table above.
- The dashboard API is down: `python3 -m fedverify.chain.push fedverify/results/demo/heart_ours_lr_demo/fallback`
  after restarting it (terminal 1), or skip to the showcase page.
- No browser or network: the showcase page `fedverify/results/showcase/index.html` works offline and walks through
  one real committed round.
